title: America.gov, the government's new assistant, scores level with GPT-5.5
paragraphs: America.gov, the General Services Administration's assistant, answers questions with AI and information from government websites. Live since September 29, it scores {agovExact}% on PolicyBench, which weights each answer by household impact and counts dollar amounts within $1 of PolicyEngine's reference and eligibility answers that match it. GPT-5.5, which OpenAI released in April, matches it at {gpt55Exact}% with AI alone and no web access, while GPT-6 Sol leads at {solExact}%, also with AI alone. America.gov would rank #{agovRank} of {nRanked} but does not join the board, which scores AI alone.

Between October 14 and 18, PolicyBench sent each of its {households} households to America.gov in a new chat, with the board's own prompt in the JSON answer format, and scored every reply as it scores the board. Six prompts run past the {charLimit} characters America.gov asks a message to stay within, so each went in as two chats asking for half the outputs apiece. Before freezing a run, PolicyBench asks a board model again when its response leaves answers out, and America.gov got the same kind of retry: each refusal went back word for word in a fresh chat, up to twice. On first attempts alone it gets {agovFirstExact}% (#{agovFirstRank}).

America.gov's first replies included {firstRefusals:words} refusals. "I cannot estimate or calculate federal or state tax, credit, payroll, or benefit amounts," it replied to the prompt for a Virginia single parent of two. Asked again, {answeredOnRetry:words} of the refusals turned into full answers and {refusedThrice:words} came back word for word the same, which leaves {unansweredRate}% of its scored answers blank; {fullModels} of the {nModels} models on the board answer every one.

America.gov gets {fedTaxRate}% of federal income tax amounts within $1, exceeding GPT-5.5's {gpt55FedTaxRate}% and trailing GPT-6 Sol's {solFedTaxRate}%, and {stateTaxRate}% of state income tax amounts, between their {gpt55StateTaxRate}% and {solStateTaxRate}%. It trails both on SNAP amounts and Medicaid eligibility. On SNAP it gets {snapRate}%, against {gpt55SnapRate}% and {solSnapRate}%, and it put a Michigan couple's SNAP at ${snap072} a year where the reference and {snap072Models} of the {nModels} models say $0. On Medicaid eligibility, the output that carries the most weight, it gets {medicaidRate}%, against {gpt55MedicaidRate}% and {solMedicaidRate}%, and it called both adults in a New York couple eligible where the reference and {medicaid004Models} models say neither is.

The current prompts define {peOutputs:words} outputs by PolicyEngine: Medicaid and CHIP eligibility "under PolicyEngine rules," and the two school-meal outputs as whether "PolicyEngine returns" support. PolicyBench is revising that wording. At least {peRefusals:words} of America.gov's {firstRefusals:words} refusals cited PolicyEngine; no model on the board declined a household on that ground, though some models' recorded reasoning notes that they cannot run PolicyEngine. Counting only the answers each gave, America.gov trails GPT-5.5 by at most {peMaxGap} points on those {peOutputs:words} outputs, and without them it would rank #{noPeRank} of {nRanked}.

PolicyBench ran this once, in one week of October. America.gov says it uses "Super Intelligence (SI) to find and explain information from official government sources," and its terms say answers generated with SI "can be incomplete or wrong." The board's last repair step, asking again for each answer still missing, one at a time, would take at least {rowRepairChats} more chats and could lift America.gov to {rowRepairMaxRate}% at most. The data below holds the replies, the scores and the method, including how PolicyBench split the long prompts.
